title: Cosmetic Labelling Requirements in India: A Panel-by-Panel Checklist for Brands
card_title: Cosmetic Labelling Requirements in India: Checklist
seo_title: Cosmetic Labelling Requirements in India: Brand Checklist
description: Cosmetic labelling requirements in India explained: Rule 34 particulars, Legal Metrology declarations, small-pack rules, claims and an artwork checklist.
image_alt: White cosmetic tubes ready for printing, showing cosmetic labelling requirements in India
body_html:
Cosmetic labelling requirements in India come from two main rulebooks, and a single carton has to satisfy both. The Cosmetics Rules, 2020 decide what a cosmetic label must say about the product, the maker and its safe use. The Legal Metrology (Packaged Commodities) Rules, 2011 decide how a packaged good is declared to a buyer: quantity, price and who to contact. Get either wrong and stock can be held back, artwork reprinted or a launch delayed. This guide walks an Indian brand founder through every element, panel by panel, with a checklist you can hand to your designer.

We are the R&D team at a third-party plant in Ambala, Haryana, and we review artwork for the brands we make for. Treat this as a practical starting point and confirm final artwork with your regulatory adviser, as rules are amended from time to time.

Who sets cosmetic labelling requirements in India

Three sets of obligations meet on one label:

  • Cosmetics Rules, 2020 (CDSCO and State Licensing Authorities). Rule 34 lists the particulars for the inner label (the bottle, tube or jar) and the outer label (the carton). Rules 36 to 39 add limits on claims and special warnings for some ingredients.
  • Legal Metrology (Packaged Commodities) Rules, 2011 (Department of Consumer Affairs and state Legal Metrology offices). Rule 6 lists the declarations every retail package needs, and Rules 7 to 9 deal with where they sit, how large they are and the language used.
  • BIS standards. Rule 34(8) of the Cosmetics Rules says labelling must also meet any labelling clause in the Indian Standard that applies to that product type under the Ninth Schedule.

The two rulebooks overlap (both want the maker’s name and the quantity), and on dates they hand over: for cosmetics, the Packaged Commodities Rules defer to the drugs and cosmetics law. That is why a cosmetic carries a use-before or expiry date.

The mandatory label elements, explained one by one

1. Name of the cosmetic

The product name must be on both the inner and outer label. Alongside your brand name, add a plain generic description (“face wash”, “hair oil”, “sunscreen lotion”), because Legal Metrology separately asks for the common or generic name of the commodity.

2. Manufacturer name and full premises address

Rule 34(1) asks for the name of the manufacturer and the complete address of the premises where the product was actually made, on both labels. In third-party manufacturing this means the plant’s name and address, with your company shown as the brand owner or marketer. Very small containers (30 g or less, or 60 ml or less) may show the manufacturer’s name with the principal place of manufacture and its pin code when the full address will not fit.

3. Use-before or expiry date

Both labels need a use-before date or date of expiry, expressed as month and year (for example, “Use before: 09/2028”). That date should come from evidence, not guesswork; our guide to cosmetic stability testing and shelf life explains how a defensible date is reached.

4. Batch number

A distinctive batch number that links back to the manufacturing record goes on the inner or outer label, preceded by a prefix such as “B. No.”, “Batch No.” or “Lot No.”. Packs of up to 10 g (solids and semi-solids) or 25 ml (liquids) are exempt, and for soaps the month and year of manufacture stands in for the batch number.

5. Manufacturing licence number

The licence number of the plant that made the product appears on the inner or outer label with a prefix such as “M.L. No.” or “Mfg. Lic. No.”. If you work on a loan licence, your own number is used instead; see our explainer on the cosmetic loan licence for when that route makes sense.

6. Net content

The outer label states the net quantity: weight for solids, volume for liquids, and either for semi-solids such as creams and gels, in metric units (g, kg, ml, l). Legal Metrology also wants it in a size you can read at a glance, with clear space around it.

7. Ingredient list

The list must open with the word “INGREDIENTS”. Ingredients present above 1% are listed in descending order of their weight or volume at the time of addition, and those at 1% or less may follow in any order. Liquid packs up to 60 ml and solid or semi-solid packs up to 30 g are exempt, though many brands still print the list on minis because buyers look for it. Use the INCI names your formulator gives you.

8. Directions, warnings and cautions

Where a product could cause harm if misused, the inner label must carry directions for safe use, any warning or caution, and the names and quantities of hazardous ingredients. Some ingredients carry their own fixed wording. Hair dyes containing p-phenylenediamine need the cautionary legend from Rule 37, which begins “Caution.—This product contains ingredients which may cause skin irritation in certain cases”, plus patch-test instructions. Soap with hexachlorophene must say “Contains hexachlorophene - not to be used on babies” (Rule 39(4)).

9. MRP, consumer care and the packer

From the Legal Metrology side, the retail package must show the maximum retail price in the form “MRP Rs ... (inclusive of all taxes)” and the name, address, telephone number and email of the person or office that handles consumer complaints. That is usually your brand’s customer care line, so set it up before you print.

Cosmetic labelling requirements by rulebook: a quick reference table

This table maps each element to its source rule and any small-pack relief.

Claims, language and the optional green dot

Claims. Rule 36 is short and strict: no cosmetic may “convey any idea which is false or misleading to the intending user”. A cosmetic cleans, beautifies or changes appearance; once a label promises to treat a disease or alter how the body works, it starts to read like a drug. In a note on common problems in import applications, CDSCO lists label phrases such as “Treatment of any disease/disorder”, “Drug Facts” and “Dermatologist recommended” as wording that may attract the definition of a drug. Keep claims to what your formula and tests support, and keep the test reports on file.

Language. Legal Metrology declarations go in English or in Hindi in Devanagari script, and a regional language can be added. Hair dye cautions under Rule 37 must appear in English and local languages.

Print size and placement. The net quantity sits on the principal display panel with clear space around it, and Rule 7 sets minimum heights for letters and numerals that grow with the pack. Use a contrasting colour, and never make a declaration readable only through the product.

Veg and non-veg dots. A green dot for vegetarian origin and a red or brown dot for non-vegetarian origin had been required on soaps, shampoos, toothpastes and other cosmetics. The Legal Metrology (Packaged Commodities) Fourth Amendment Rules, 2026, notified on 21 September 2026, moved this to the list of optional declarations, so you may still print it at the top of the front panel but it is no longer compulsory. If you use it, every ingredient, including fragrance and emulsifier sources, must back up the colour.

A step-by-step artwork approval workflow

Most label errors start when artwork is finished before the formula and pack are locked.

  1. Lock the formula and pack. The ingredient list, net quantity, directions and warnings all depend on the final formula and container.
  2. Get a label text pack from the manufacturer. Ask R&D for the INCI list in the right order, the recommended directions and cautions, the shelf life and the exact manufacturer name, address and licence number.
  3. Build artwork on the real dieline. Your printer’s dieline shows panels, folds and glue flaps, so nothing compulsory ends up under a flap or seam.
  4. Leave blank spaces for variable data. Batch number, use-before date and often the MRP are printed or coded at filling. Agree the coding area and its background colour with the plant.
  5. Check against a written checklist. Tick every element in the table above, plus spelling of the plant address and licence number.
  6. Sign a final proof. Both the brand and the manufacturer should sign the proof before the print order. The licensee must report a labelling change to its Licensing Authority within thirty days (Rule 26(k)), so later edits have a cost.

Common label mistakes we see, and how to avoid them

  • Brand address printed as the manufacturer. In third-party production, the manufacturer line must name the plant that made the product.
  • Ingredients in random order or with marketing names (“rose extract”) in place of INCI names.
  • No space left for batch and date coding, forcing stickers that look untidy and may not be allowed for compulsory declarations.
  • MRP stickers covering the printed MRP. Rule 6(3) of the Packaged Commodities Rules lets a sticker lower the price but not hide the original one.
  • Drug-like claims such as “cures acne” or “treats hair fall”.

How Ecosmetix supports labelling for brands

For private label and custom projects, packaging selection, artwork support and compliance checks are part of our process, right after sample approval and before production. Our R&D team supplies the ingredient declaration, directions and cautions for each formula from our range of 100+ graded formulas (Grade 1 to Grade 4), and our plant details and licence number for the manufacturer line. Lab samples are typically ready in about 14 days, so your designer can work on artwork while you test the product. With 16,000 kg a day of mixing and up to 60,000 tubes a day of filling in Ambala, and delivery across India, the label is often what holds a launch back, so we start on it early. If you are still comparing partners, our guide on third-party cosmetic manufacturing covers the wider process.

faqs.q: What is mandatory on a cosmetic label in India?
faqs.a: Under Rule 34 of the Cosmetics Rules, 2020, the label needs the product name, the manufacturer’s name and premises address, a use-before or expiry date in month and year, a batch number, the manufacturing licence number, net content, an ingredient list headed “INGREDIENTS”, and safe-use directions or warnings where relevant. The Legal Metrology rules add the MRP inclusive of all taxes and consumer care contact details.

faqs.q: Is an ingredient list compulsory on cosmetics in India?
faqs.a: Yes, for most packs. Rule 34(7) asks for ingredients above 1% in descending order, then the rest in any order, under the word “INGREDIENTS”. Liquid packs of 60 ml or less and solid or semi-solid packs of 30 g or less are exempt, though printing the list on them is good practice.

faqs.q: Is an expiry date mandatory on cosmetics in India?
faqs.a: Yes. Both the inner and outer label must show a use-before date or date of expiry in month and year. The date should be supported by stability data for that formula in that pack.

faqs.q: Whose name goes on the label in third party manufacturing?
faqs.a: The manufacturer line shows the name and full premises address of the plant that actually made the product, with that plant’s manufacturing licence number. Your company appears as the brand owner or marketer.

faqs.q: Is the green veg dot mandatory on cosmetics?
faqs.a: Not any more. The Legal Metrology (Packaged Commodities) Fourth Amendment Rules, 2026, notified on 21 September 2026, made the green and red or brown dot an optional declaration for soaps, shampoos, toothpastes and other cosmetics. If you print it, it goes at the top of the principal display panel.

faqs.q: Can a cosmetic label be only in English?
faqs.a: Legal Metrology declarations may be in English or in Hindi in Devanagari script, so an English label meets that rule. Certain warnings, such as the hair dye caution under Rule 37, must also appear in local languages.

faqs.q: Can I put a sticker on a cosmetic label to change the MRP?
faqs.a: A sticker may be used to reduce the MRP, but it must not cover the original printed price. Stickers cannot be used to change or add compulsory declarations, so plan the printed label carefully.

faqs.q: What claims are not allowed on cosmetic labels?
faqs.a: Rule 36 bars any false or misleading claim. Words that suggest treating a disease or changing the structure or function of the body can make a product look like a drug; CDSCO has flagged phrases such as “Drug Facts” and “Dermatologist recommended” in its review notes. Claims should be backed by test data.
